newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croats, Serbs mark US-brokered peace anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Croats, Serbs mark US-brokered peace anniversary.

text.p: A U.S. envoy urged Croatia and its Serb minority on Tuesday to bury the past and make peace a year after their leaders signed a landmark agreement ending the four-year Serb rebellion in Eastern Slavonia.
"Reconciliation requires both Croats and Serbs to accept the reality of the present situation," U.S. Ambassador to Croatia Peter Galbraith said.
"Both communities have suffered and neither community deserved what happened to it," he told journalists in Eastern Slavonia, the last Serb-controlled area of Croatia.
Thousands of people were killed or expelled from the region that saw some of the worst fighting in a six-month war sparked by Croatia's bid for independence from ex-Yugoslavia in 1991.
Officials and journalists gathered at a brief ceremony in the town of Erdut to mark the first anniversary of the signing of the U.S.-brokered peace agreement.
The accord put an end to a Serb rebellion and enabled Croatia to restore its rule over Eastern Slavonia after an interim period under United Nations authority.
It also guarantees 100,000 Croat inhabitants driven out of the region the right to return, while Serbs who lived there when the war erupted could retain their homes.
The Croatian army recaptured two other Serb enclaves in blitz offensives in 1995, causing a Serb exodus from the areas.
According to U.N. figures, 60,000 Serbs from other areas in Croatia found refuge in Eastern Slavonia, while some 120,000 others fled to Bosnia and Yugoslavia.
The region is now under control of the U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES), endowed with 5,000 troops and a mandate to create conditions for a gradual restoration of Croatian rule.
The mandate originally expires in January, but last week Croatia agreed to its six-month extension and said it would allow U.N observers to stay for another six months.
Galbraith said that 20,000 Eastern Slavonia residents, most of them Serbs, have applied for Croatian citizenship issued in six documentation centres recently opened in the area.

"I want to go home...I will stay here only if I have to... everybody's heart is at his own home," said Simo Rusovo, 56, from Donji Lapac in central Croatia who has been queueing in front of a documentation centre since the early morning.
But as inter-ethnic tensions remain high, not a single Croatian refugee has so far returned to Eastern Slavonia.
Very few Serbs ventured to go back to the Krajina region which was their home for centuries and from which they had expelled their Croat neighbours during their four-year rule.
Journalists taken on a tour of Eastern Slavonia were shown four villages already handed back to Croatians where authorities expect up to 300 people to return by Christmas.
The villages were deserted. Only people there were Croatian experts carrying out reconstruction and demining work.
"The owner of the house where I live now has the right to come back," said 40-year-old Jovanka Jovanovic, a widowed mother of five.
Five years ago she fled Vocin in Croatia before advancing government troops and is now living in a Croatian home in the village of Nijemci, recently turned over to the Croatian side.
"I hope my problem will be solved one day too...But there are no Serbs left in my hometown... and I wouldn't dare to be the first to go back," she said.
With mistrust still running high, many observers fear Croat-Serb reconciliation will never happen.
"There is a possibility that a large percentage of people will leave, if their basic rights and freedoms are not guaranteed," local Serb leader Vojislav Stanimirovic said.
"This country will survive only if people reconcile and if they return to their old homes," he told Reuters.
